Chapter 8: The Rollercoaster of Self-Care
You know, self-care gets mentioned everywhere these days. But if you’re living with mental illness, you already know—it’s not as easy as lighting a candle or soaking in a bubble bath.
Some days, self-care is just managing to get yourself out of bed. Other days, it’s saying no to plans you just can’t handle, or reaching out for help, or even just forgiving yourself for having a tough time.
Picture someone sitting with a prescription bottle in their hands, silently weighing whether to take their medication. The side effects are annoying. The routine gets old. But skipping a dose? That’s not really an option. It hits you—self-care isn’t always pretty, or something you’d post about online. Sometimes, it’s just doing whatever you need to make it through the day.
And here’s something most people don’t realize: self-care comes with a lot of guilt. There’s this pressure to do it “perfectly,” to always be making progress, to never let anyone down. But for folks living with mental illness, self-care isn’t about impressing anyone. It’s about survival.
Imagine someone who’s been struggling for weeks, finally working up the courage to call their therapist. There’s instant relief, but also this wave of shame—shouldn’t they be able to handle things on their own? But over time, it becomes clear: asking for help isn’t a weakness. It’s a real sign of strength.
Self-care can also show up in tiny, unexpected moments—a favorite song playing when you need it most, a quiet walk outside, or just a warm cup of tea in your hands. These moments might not solve everything, but they give you a little breathing room in the middle of a storm. You realize self-care isn’t about being perfect. It’s about being kind—to yourself, most of all.
Living with mental illness means you learn to tune in to what you really need, even when it doesn’t make sense to anyone else. It’s about forgiving yourself for the hard days, and celebrating the good ones—no matter how small. And in the end, self-care stops being about doing things “right.” It’s about figuring out what actually helps you, and letting that be enough.
